answer: A habit I would genuinely like to give up is my tendency to procrastinate, especially with tasks I find unpleasant. Paperwork is the worst example; I will happily reply to twenty student messages to avoid filling in one boring form. It started, I think, as a way of avoiding stress, but over time it has become quite [[ingrained]]. At university I often left assignments until the night before, and because I usually got away with it, I never learned to change. I want to give it up because it often leaves me rushing at the last minute, which is both stressful and [[counterproductive]]. I know that if I tackled things sooner, my life would be far calmer and more organised. It also isn't fair on my colleagues when they have to wait for my part of the work. To break the habit, I have started using to-do lists and breaking large tasks into smaller, more [[manageable]] steps. I have also tried the technique of simply starting a task for five minutes, which often removes the initial reluctance. Once I begin, I usually realise the task is not nearly as bad as I had imagined. I have also started tackling the task I dread most first thing in the morning, while my energy is high. Honestly, procrastination is a surprisingly [[stubborn]] habit to break, and I have to remain constantly [[vigilant]]. Still, I have made real progress, and I feel much better when I stay on top of things. It is a work in progress, but one I am fully committed to.

followUps.q: Do other people in your family procrastinate?
followUps.answer: Not really, which makes it more embarrassing! My younger sister is incredibly disciplined and finishes her work days early. She often teases me about it, which is actually good motivation.

followUps.q: Is procrastination always a bad thing?
followUps.answer: Mostly, yes, but occasionally a little delay helps, because ideas have time to develop. The problem is when it becomes a [[chronic]] pattern and you are always working under pressure.
